pages.title: TrackIt — Product Overview
pages.content:
What TrackIt is

TrackIt is a company-wide work tracking system. It connects the organisation's structure to the work being done and the time being spent, so that managers can answer questions about progress and capacity from one place instead of three spreadsheets.

The first version is a task and resource tracking application. It can later expand into a full company project-tracking platform.

The problem

Software companies commonly track tasks, employee time, project goals and team allocation in separate tools. Because the data is split, managers struggle to answer basic questions:

- What is each team currently working on?
- Is a project on schedule?
- Which employees are overloaded, and which are underutilised?
- How much time has been spent on each task?
- Which tasks are delayed or high risk?
- Are team goals progressing toward their deadlines?

Employees have a parallel problem: work arrives through chat messages and meetings, with no single place to see what is assigned to them or record what they did.

The model

Everything in TrackIt hangs off one chain:

Company
  └── Teams
       └── Team Goals
            └── Tasks
                 └── Assigned Employees
                      └── Daily Timesheets
                           └── Progress and Resource Dashboards

A goal is a body of work with a deadline, owned by one team. Tasks are the assignable units under a goal. Time is recorded against tasks. Everything a dashboard shows is derived from that chain.

Roles

Role | What they do
Super Admin | Creates teams, users and team leads. Sees every team, goal, task and timesheet, plus company-wide resource allocation.
Team Lead | Creates goals for their team, breaks them into tasks, assigns members, sets priorities, and monitors their team's progress, timesheets and workload.
Employee | Sees only their assigned tasks. Updates task status, records daily time with a short work note, and views their own timesheet history.

A Manager, in the language of the original requirements, is served by the Team Lead and Super Admin views rather than being a separate role.

What success looks like

TrackIt is working when:

- A Super Admin can build the company structure and see allocation across every team
- A Team Lead can create a goal with a deadline, assign the work, and see who is overloaded
- An Employee has one screen showing what is assigned to them and one place to log time
- Overdue, blocked and high-risk work is visible without anyone having to go looking for it

Related pages

- Product Requirements — the scoped feature set
- Roadmap — phasing and sequence
- System Architecture — how it is built

Note on this project

TrackIt is a demonstration application. It is built to exercise a realistic set of engineering problems — role-based access, effort tracking, dependency graphs, derived metrics — and to produce a body of interlinked project data.

pages.title: TrackIt — Product Requirements
pages.content:
Purpose

This page defines what TrackIt does, feature by feature, and what it deliberately does not do. It is the reference for scope questions during the build.

Delivery is organised into six epics, tracked in Jira project TRACKIT.

Permissions summary

Capability | Super Admin | Team Lead | Employee
Create teams and users | Yes | No | No
Assign team leads | Yes | No | No
Create goals and tasks | Yes | Own team | No
Assign tasks | Yes | Own team | No
Update task status | Yes | Own team | Own tasks
Log time | — | — | Own tasks
View timesheets | All | Own team | Own only
View allocation dashboards | Company-wide | Own team | No

The rule that governs every row: scope is enforced server-side, in the query. Hiding a control in the interface is not access control.

Epic 1 — Team and user administration

A Super Admin creates users with a name, email, password and role, creates teams, adds employees to teams, and designates exactly one team lead per team. Login uses JWT; role-based middleware guards every protected route.

Accepted when: the Super Admin can build the full structure; exactly one lead exists per team; an employee calling an admin endpoint receives 403.

Epic 2 — Goals, tasks and assignment

A Team Lead creates a goal for their team with a start date, deadline and importance, then breaks it into tasks carrying a priority, an estimated effort and a due date. Tasks are assigned to members of that same team. Employees see their assigned tasks on one screen and move them between statuses. Each goal shows a progress percentage derived from its completed tasks.

Statuses — Goal: PLANNED, ACTIVE, COMPLETED, CANCELLED. Task: TODO, IN_PROGRESS, BLOCKED, DONE. Priority: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH.

Accepted when: a lead can create a goal and tasks and assign them; an employee sees only their own tasks and can change their status; goal progress reflects completed tasks.

Epic 3 — Employee timesheets

An employee records hours against an assigned task for a given date, with a short work note. Time cannot be logged against a task that is not assigned to them. Hours are validated against a configured daily maximum and cannot be zero, negative or future-dated. Employees can correct or delete their own entries and review their history over a date range. Each task shows total recorded time against its estimate.

Accepted when: time can be logged only against assigned tasks; invalid hours are rejected; task detail shows actual against estimated effort; no employee can see another's entries.

Epic 4 — Resource allocation and dashboards

One calculation determines each employee's utilisation:

utilisation = estimated hours on active tasks / weekly capacity

  0–60%  Available
 61–90%  Balanced
   >90%  Overloaded

Weekly capacity is configurable per team, defaulting to 40 hours. An active task is one that is not DONE; blocked tasks still count, because blocked work still occupies a person.

The Team Dashboard shows goal and task KPIs plus a per-employee workload table. The Super Admin sees the same shape company-wide, with filters for team, employee and date range.

Accepted when: a lead sees allocation for their own team only; the Super Admin sees all teams; overloaded and available employees are visible; an employee with no tasks still appears in the table.

Epic 5 — Prioritisation and dependencies

Tasks can declare that they depend on other tasks. Self-dependencies and circular dependencies are rejected. A task is blocked when a prerequisite is not yet DONE.

Ranking uses a fixed, published formula:

Priority score =
  Business priority + Deadline urgency
+ Dependency impact + Goal importance
- Blocked penalty

High priority:       +30      Due within 2 days:   +30
Medium priority:     +20      Due within 7 days:   +20
Low priority:        +10      Due later:            +5

Blocks another task: +10 each
Currently blocked:   -40

Every recommendation carries the reasons behind its score. An unexplained ranking is one nobody trusts, so the explanation is part of the feature rather than decoration on it.

Accepted when: cycles are rejected; blocked tasks are identified; available tasks are ranked; a lead can see why a task scored as it did.

Epic 6 — Risk, audit and search

Eight conditions raise a risk: task overdue, high-priority task blocked, goal deadline approaching, goal progress below expectation, unassigned task, employee overloaded, actual hours exceeding estimate, and no recent progress. Risks are grouped by severity and link through to the underlying record.

Significant changes — status, assignment, priority, timesheets, goals, dependencies — are written to an activity log. Tasks are searchable and filterable, and users are notified in-app when work is assigned to them.

Accepted when: risks appear in one place with severity; important actions appear in history; tasks can be searched within the caller's scope.

Out of scope

- Email, Slack or push notifications — in-app only
- Approval workflows for timesheets
- Billing, invoicing, payroll or cost rates
- Predictive or machine-learning risk scoring; all rules are deterministic
- Automatic assignment or scheduling — the system recommends, a human decides
- Password reset, email verification, SSO, multi-tenancy
- Critical-path analysis and Gantt scheduling

Open decisions

Five choices remain open and are recorded on the Architecture Decision Records page. Two of them block the first migration: whether a user can belong to more than one team, and whether a task can have more than one assignee.

pages.title: TrackIt — Roadmap
pages.content:
Shape of the plan

Six sprints, one epic each. Each sprint is scheduled as one week, though the intent is to complete most in two to three days.

The sequence is dictated by data dependencies rather than preference: you cannot log time against a task that does not exist, and you cannot calculate workload without estimates and recorded hours. Each sprint's output is the next sprint's input.

Sprints

# | Dates | Sprint | Goal
1 | Aug 10–14 | Foundation & Org Structure | A Super Admin can log in, build the company structure, and every role boundary is enforced server-side. The layered pattern is established and copyable.
2 | Aug 17–21 | Goals, Tasks & Assignment | A Team Lead can create a goal, break it into tasks and assign them; an Employee sees only their own work. Goal progress reflects reality.
3 | Aug 24–28 | Time Recording | Employees record daily hours against assigned tasks, and every task shows actual effort against its estimate.
4 | Aug 31–Sep 4 | Resource Visibility | A Team Lead can see who is overloaded and who is free; a Super Admin can compare teams. One workload calculation, used everywhere.
5 | Sep 7–11 | Prioritisation & Dependencies | Tasks can depend on each other without cycles, and the system recommends what to do next with reasons a human can check.
6 | Sep 14–18 | Risk, Audit & Polish | Delivery risks surface in one place before deadlines are missed, significant changes are recorded, and the app is demo-ready.

Deliverable at each phase

Phase 1 (Sprints 1–2) — a working role-based task management application. Structure, goals, tasks, assignments, deadlines and progress can all be managed.

Phase 2 (Sprints 3–4) — employees record daily work; leads and admins can inspect timesheets, task effort, team workload and resource allocation.

Phase 3 (Sprints 5–6) — the application ranks tasks, detects blockers, highlights resource and deadline risks, records important changes, and provides management dashboards.

Story distribution

Sprint | Stories | Jira
1 | 7 | TRACKIT-12 → 18
2 | 5 | TRACKIT-19 → 23
3 | 4 | TRACKIT-24 → 27
4 | 3 | TRACKIT-28 → 30
5 | 4 | TRACKIT-31 → 34
6 | 4 | TRACKIT-35 → 38

Sprint 1 is the heaviest: it carries the whole project bootstrap alongside authentication and team administration. It is the sprint most likely to overrun, and the scaffold work is the part to timebox hardest.

Sprint 4 is the lightest at three stories, but two of them are dashboards, and dashboard work tends to expand to fill the time available.

Sequencing constraints

These are hard, not preferences:

- Nothing can be authorised until identity exists (Sprint 1 blocks everything)
- Time attaches to tasks, so tasks precede timesheets
- Workload needs both estimates and recorded hours, so allocation follows time recording
- Priority scoring needs blocked state, which needs dependencies
- Risk detection consumes all four preceding epics and must be last

If time runs short

Cut in this order, from the least costly:

1. Optional polish — dark mode, drag-and-drop, CSV export, charts
2. Search and filtering
3. Notifications
4. Activity logging

Risk detection is what makes Phase 3 meaningful and is the last thing to go. Everything in Phases 1 and 2 is load-bearing.

Details include the resolved lead, the members list, and memberCount. - Add member — the user must exist (404) and be an EMPLOYEE (409). One-team-per-user is enforced: already in this team, or already in another team → 409. - Assign lead — the target must already be a member (409). The repository does this transactionally with a pessimistic lock: promote the new user to TEAM_LEAD, demote the previous lead back to EMPLOYEE, and update teams.lead_id — three writes that must not interleave with another assignment. - Remove member — must be a current member (404); the current lead cannot be removed until another lead is assigned (409). 7.4 Goal management (TRACKIT-19) flowchart TB Page["TeamGoalsPage.tsx"] -->|"GET /teams"| TeamPicker["Team selector — Super Admin"] Page --> GoalForm["GoalCreationForm"] GoalForm -->|"POST /goals"| Created["Planned goal"] Page -->|"GET /teams/:teamId/goals?status="| Goals["Goals with progress"] Details["GoalDetailsPage.tsx"] -->|"GET /goals/:id"| Goal["Goal + progress + status breakdown"] - UI: pages/TeamGoalsPage.tsx, GoalDetailsPage.tsx, components/GoalCreationForm.tsx, GoalStatusBadge.tsx, GoalProgress.tsx, goal-display.ts (deadline countdown / overdue text). - Create goal — assertCanManageTeam; the deadline must fall strictly after the start date (400 otherwise); a new goal is always PLANNED; createdById is stamped from the caller, never from the body. - List — assertCanViewTeam, ordered by deadline then title, optional ?status= filter. Progress for every goal in the list is loaded in one grouped query (countByGoalIdsAndStatus) — an explicit N+1 avoidance, and the reason GoalService is allowed to touch TaskRepository directly. - Get / update — the 404-then-403 pattern. Update accepts a partial body (at least one field) and re-validates dates against the merged start/deadline, so changing only the start date still cannot invert the range. - Importance (LOW | MEDIUM | HIGH) is stored but not yet consumed — it feeds priority scoring in Phase 3. 7.5 Task creation & editing (TRACKIT-20) flowchart TB Details["GoalDetailsPage.tsx"] --> Form["TaskCreationForm"] Form -->|"POST /goals/:goalId/tasks"| Created["TODO, unassigned task"] Details --> List["TaskList"] List -->|"GET /goals/:goalId/tasks"| Tasks["Role-scoped tasks"] List -->|"PATCH /tasks/:id"| Updated["Updated task"] TaskPage["TaskDetailsPage.tsx"] -->|"GET /tasks/:id"| Task["Task projection"] - UI: components/TaskCreationForm.tsx, TaskList.tsx, TaskStatusBadges.tsx, and pages/TaskDetailsPage.tsx (single-task view with assignment controls for a Team Lead). - Create task — resolves the parent goal through goalService.getGoal (which authorises the caller), then assertCanManageTeam. Estimated hours must be > 0 (400). New tasks start TODO, unassigned, with businessImpact and priorityScore null. - A due date after the goal's deadline is allowed but flagged. The projection carries dueDatePastGoalDeadline so the UI can warn without blocking — a real plan sometimes needs a task that outruns its goal, and the person should see it, not be stopped by it. - Update task — partial body, assertCanManageTeam, re-validates the estimate if changed. Bodies are .strict(), so unknown fields are rejected rather than silently ignored. 7.6 Task assignment (TRACKIT-21) flowchart LR Row["TaskList row or TaskDetailsPage"] --> Select["AssigneeSelect"] Select -->|"PUT /tasks/:id/assignee
{ assigneeId or null }"| Task["Updated task"] flowchart TB A["PUT /tasks/:id/assignee"] --> B{"requireRole(TEAM_LEAD)"} B -->|"no"| E1["403"] B -->|"yes"| C{"task exists?"} C -->|"no"| E2["404"] C -->|"yes"| D["getGoal → team scope"] D --> F{"assertTeamLeadOf(caller, goal.teamId)"} F -->|"no"| E3["403"] F -->|"yes"| G{"assigneeId null?"} G -->|"yes"| I["unassign"] G -->|"no"| H{"assertMemberOf(assigneeId, goal.teamId)"} H -->|"no"| E4["403 — not on this team"] H -->|"yes"| I2["assign"] The assertMemberOf check is what enforces the domain invariant a task's assignee is a member of the team owning the task's goal. AssigneeSelect renders only when canAssign (Team Lead); the member list comes from GET /teams/:teamId. 7.7 My Tasks & status updates (TRACKIT-22) flowchart TB Page["MyTasksPage.tsx"] --> Controls["Status / due-before filters
deadline / priority sort"] Controls -->|"GET /tasks/mine?status=&dueBefore="| Tasks["Caller's tasks with parent goals"] Page --> Status["TaskStatusSelect"] Status -->|"PATCH /tasks/:id/status"| Updated["Updated task"] - GET /tasks/mine — findByAssignee(callerId, filter) returns only the caller's tasks, inner-joined to the parent goal so each row already carries goal.{ id, title }. No second request, no N+1. Filters are applied in SQL; ordered by due date then title. - PATCH /tasks/:id/status is role-branched — the one task write an Employee can perform: flowchart LR S["PATCH /tasks/:id/status"] --> R{"caller role"} R -->|"SUPER_ADMIN"| OK["update"] R -->|"TEAM_LEAD"| TS["getGoal → assertTeamLeadOf"] --> OK R -->|"EMPLOYEE"| A{"task has an assignee?"} A -->|"no"| F1["403"] A -->|"yes"| B{"assertOwnsResource(caller, assigneeId)"} B -->|"no"| F2["403"] B -->|"yes"| OK - Sorting is client-side (components/my-task-sorting.ts): priority HIGH→LOW then deadline, or deadline then title. It is presentation, so it stays in the browser. 7.8 Goal progress from tasks (TRACKIT-23) progress = tasks with status DONE / total tasks × 100 (computed on read, never stored) - Computed from a single grouped count of tasks by status — countByGoalAndStatus for one goal, countByGoalIdsAndStatus for a list. - A goal with no tasks reports progress: 0 with noTasksYet: true, so the UI shows "No tasks yet" rather than a misleading 0%. - Every projection carries the full taskStatusBreakdown so GoalProgress.tsx renders the bar and the counts without another call. The API returns an exact percentage; the component rounds it for display. - Counted, not weighted by hours — a known, accepted simplification (DOMAIN.md §Goal progress). On the goal details page, creating or completing a task triggers a re-fetch of the goal to refresh the bar. 7.9 The whole journey, one diagram sequenceDiagram autonumber actor SA as Super Admin actor TL as Team Lead (Priya) actor EM as Employee (Alex) participant API as TrackIt API Note over SA,API: Sprint 1 — build the company SA->>API: POST /users — create Priya, Alex SA->>API: POST /teams — "Platform Team" SA->>API: POST /teams/:id/members — add Alex, add Priya SA->>API: PUT /teams/:id/lead — promote Priya to TEAM_LEAD Note over TL,API: Sprint 2 — plan and do the work TL->>API: POST /goals — "Ship v1" (PLANNED, HIGH) TL->>API: POST /goals/:id/tasks — "Set up CI" (TODO, unassigned) TL->>API: PUT /tasks/:id/assignee — { assigneeId: Alex } Note right of API: assertMemberOf(Alex, Platform Team) EM->>API: GET /tasks/mine API-->>EM: only Alex's tasks, each with its goal EM->>API: PATCH /tasks/:id/status — IN_PROGRESS EM->>API: PATCH /tasks/:id/status — DONE Note right of API: assertOwnsResource(Alex, task.assigneeId) TL->>API: GET /goals/:id API-->>TL: progress recomputed from task counts 8. API reference All responses are JSON. Errors use { "error": { "message": "..." } }. Dates are strict YYYY-MM-DD strings, validated at the boundary. Every route except /auth/login and /health requires Authorization: Bearer . Auth & infrastructure Method | Path | Access | Request | Success | Notable errors POST | /auth/login | public | { email, password } | 200 { token, user } | 401 invalid credentials GET | /auth/me | authenticated | — | 200 { user } | 401 GET | /health | public | — | 200 { status, database } | 503 database down Users Method | Path | Access | Request | Success | Notable errors POST | /users | SUPER_ADMIN | { name, email, password, role } | 201 { user } | 400, 401, 403, 409 duplicate email GET | /users | SUPER_ADMIN | query role?, unassigned? | 200 { users } | 401, 403 Teams Method | Path | Access | Request | Success | Notable errors POST | /teams | SUPER_ADMIN | { name, description?, weeklyCapacityHours? } | 201 { team } | 401, 403, 409 duplicate name GET | /teams | authenticated | — | 200 { teams } (role-scoped) | 401 GET | /teams/:id | authenticated | — | 200 { team } (lead, members, memberCount) | 401, 403, 404 POST | /teams/:id/members | SUPER_ADMIN | { userId } | 201 { member } | 401, 403, 404, 409 DELETE | /teams/:id/members/:userId | SUPER_ADMIN | — | 204 | 401, 403, 404, 409 lead not reassigned PUT | /teams/:id/lead | SUPER_ADMIN | { userId } | 200 { lead } | 401, 403, 404, 409 not a member Goals Method | Path | Access | Request | Success | Notable errors POST | /goals | SUPER_ADMIN, TEAM_LEAD | { teamId, title, description?, startDate, deadline, importance } | 201 { goal } | 400 dates, 401, 403 GET | /teams/:teamId/goals | authenticated | query status? | 200 { goals } (with progress) | 401, 403 GET | /goals/:id | authenticated | — | 200 { goal } (progress + breakdown) | 401, 403, 404 PATCH | /goals/:id | SUPER_ADMIN, TEAM_LEAD | partial { title?, description?, startDate?, deadline?, status?, importance? } | 200 { goal } | 400, 401, 403, 404 Tasks Method | Path | Access | Request | Success | Notable errors POST | /goals/:goalId/tasks | SUPER_ADMIN, TEAM_LEAD | { title, description?, priority, estimatedHours, dueDate } | 201 { task } | 400 estimate, 401, 403, 404 GET | /goals/:goalId/tasks | authenticated | — | 200 { tasks } (role-scoped) | 401, 403, 404 GET | /tasks/mine | authenticated | query status?, dueBefore? | 200 { tasks } (with parent goal) | 400, 401 GET | /tasks/:id | authenticated | — | 200 { task } | 401, 403, 404 PATCH | /tasks/:id | SUPER_ADMIN, TEAM_LEAD | partial { title?, description?, priority?, estimatedHours?, dueDate? } | 200 { task } | 400, 401, 403, 404 PATCH | /tasks/:id/status | authenticated (role-branched) | { status } | 200 { task } | 401, 403, 404 PUT | /tasks/:id/assignee | TEAM_LEAD | { assigneeId \| null } | 200 { task } | 401, 403, 404 9. Running & verifying end to end With Docker Compose (recommended) cp backend/.env.example backend/.env # first time only docker compose up - Frontend: http://localhost:5173 - API: http://localhost:3000 - PostgreSQL: localhost:5432 On the host # backend cd backend && cp .env.example .env && npm install && npm run dev # frontend (separate shell) — set VITE_API_URL to the API base URL cd frontend && npm install && npm run dev JWT_SECRET must be at least 32 characters; env vars are validated at boot (backend/src/common/config/env.ts), so a misconfigured environment fails immediately rather than at the first request. Migrate and seed cd backend npm run migration:run # applies all seven migrations npm run seed The seed (backend/src/scripts/seeds/company-structure.seed.ts) is idempotent — records are keyed by email and team name, so a second run changes nothing. It creates 2 teams and 9 users; every account's password is TrackIt123!: Name | Role | Team | Email TrackIt Admin | Super Admin | — | admin@trackit.local Priya | Team Lead | Platform Team | priya@trackit.local Alex | Employee | Platform Team | alex@trackit.local Maya | Employee | Platform Team | maya@trackit.local Jordan | Employee | Platform Team | jordan@trackit.local Diego | Employee | Platform Team | diego@trackit.local Sam | Team Lead | Frontend Team | sam@trackit.local Elena | Employee | Frontend Team | elena@trackit.local Noah | Employee | Frontend Team | noah@trackit.local The seed creates no goals or tasks — those are created through the UI or the API, so the Sprint 2 flow is exercised for real rather than pre-baked. Verify the API from the command line # health — proves route → database curl http://localhost:3000/health # → {"status":"ok","database":"up"} # log in as a Team Lead TOKEN=$(curl -s http://localhost:3000/auth/login \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"email":"priya@trackit.local","password":"TrackIt123!"}' | jq -r .token) # scoped team list — Priya sees only the team she leads TEAM=$(curl -s http://localhost:3000/teams -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq -r '.teams[0].id') # create a goal under that team GOAL=$(curl -s http://localhost:3000/goals -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{\"teamId\":\"$TEAM\",\"title\":\"Ship v1\",\"startDate\":\"2026-08-01\",\"deadline\":\"2026-09-01\",\"importance\":\"HIGH\"}" \ | jq -r .goal.id) # add a task, then read the goal back to see progress curl -s http://localhost:3000/goals/$GOAL/tasks -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"title":"Set up CI","priority":"HIGH","estimatedHours":8,"dueDate":"2026-08-15"}' curl http://localhost:3000/goals/$GOAL -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" # → progress 0, noTasksYet false, taskStatusBreakdown.total 1 Verify in the browser 1. As Super Admin (admin@trackit.local) — open Users and Teams: create a user, create a team, add employees, assign a lead. 2. As Team Lead (priya@trackit.local) — the team list is scoped to her team only. Open Goals and Tasks: create a goal, open it, add tasks, assign one to Alex, and watch progress move as you mark a task DONE. 3. As Employee (alex@trackit.local) — Team Goals shows the team's goals read-only, and My Tasks shows only Alex's assigned tasks with a status selector. That last point is the query-level scoping, visible. Tests cd backend && npm test # 161 tests, all passing cd frontend && node --test src/**/*.test.ts # navigation, goal display, my-task sorting Backend coverage spans all four layers of every module — auth, users, teams, goals, tasks — plus the middleware, ScopeService, and the seed's idempotency. 10. Known limitations & follow-ups Accepted trade-offs - Progress is counted, not weighted. A goal with one 40-hour task and nine 1-hour tasks reads 90% done when the small ones finish. Accepted for simplicity (DOMAIN.md §Goal progress). - Goal status is manual by design. Never derived from task counts, so a goal at 100% progress stays ACTIVE until a human marks it COMPLETED — which keeps CANCELLED a deliberate decision. - JWT inlocalStorage. Convenient for this simulation and survives reloads, but exposed to XSS. Refresh tokens and production-grade cookie sessions are deliberately out of scope. - No deletion of goals or tasks. They can be created and updated but not deleted via the API; the RESTRICT foreign keys anticipate this being a deliberate future operation rather than a cascade. Inert by design — reserved for later phases - Task.businessImpact and Task.priorityScore are always null, and Goal.importance / Task.priority are stored but never combined into a score. The constants.ts scoring tunables are unused. - No task dependencies. The TaskDependency / blocked-by model from DOMAIN.md has no table or endpoints; BLOCKED today is only a manually set lifecycle status. - No time logging. estimatedHours exists but there is no way to record actual hours. - Team.weeklyCapacityHours is stored and settable but nothing consumes it yet — utilisation and workload are Phase 2. Known drift - The root README.md "Running the frontend" section still describes the Vite proxy (VITE_API_TARGET) removed by TRACKIT-39. The frontend now calls the API directly via VITE_API_URL. What Phase 2 picks up (TRACKIT-24 → 30) Timesheet entries against tasks, effort variance (recorded − estimated), utilisation and workload classification against Team.weeklyCapacityHours, and the first dashboards. Every one of those builds directly on what is documented above: tasks.estimatedHours, tasks.assigneeId, and the team scope model.

pages.title: TrackIt — System Architecture
pages.content:
Technology stack

Frontend:       React + TypeScript
Backend:        Node.js + Express + TypeScript
Database:       PostgreSQL
ORM:            TypeORM
Authentication: JWT
Validation:     Zod
API style:      REST
Development:    Docker Compose

Modular monolith

TrackIt is a single deployable backend divided into modules. Microservices were considered and rejected — the operational overhead of separate services buys nothing at this size, and the whole application shares one database and one transaction boundary anyway.

backend/
├── auth/
├── users/
├── teams/
├── goals/
├── tasks/
├── timesheets/
├── dashboards/
└── audit/

Modules are boundaries of responsibility, not deployment. They can be extracted later if a real reason appears.

Layered design

Every module follows the same four-layer shape:

module/
├── <module>.controller.ts   HTTP boundary: routing, request/response, Zod validation
├── <module>.service.ts      business logic, authorisation rules, orchestration
├── <module>.repository.ts   data access, TypeORM queries
└── <module>.entity.ts       TypeORM entity definitions

The rules:

- Controllers never touch repositories directly
- Business rules live in services, not controllers
- Cross-module reads go through the other module's service, not its repository
- Validation happens at the controller boundary; authorisation happens in the service

Project structure

src/
├── modules/
│   └── <module>/
│       ├── <module>.controller.ts
│       ├── <module>.service.ts
│       ├── <module>.repository.ts
│       └── <module>.entity.ts
├── common/
│   ├── errors/
│   ├── middleware/
│   └── config/
└── data-source.ts

Authorisation

Authorisation lives in exactly two places:

Role checks at the route. requireAuth verifies the JWT and attaches req.user. requireRole(...roles) rejects an insufficient role. Routes declare their requirement declaratively.

Scope checks in the service, because they need data:

- assertTeamLeadOf(userId, teamId)
- assertMemberOf(userId, teamId)
- assertOwnsResource(userId, resourceOwnerId)

The moment a controller starts inspecting req.user.role, the pattern has broken.

Error contract: missing, expired or malformed token → 401. Valid token but insufficient role or scope → 403. A resource outside the caller's scope returns 403 rather than 404 — chosen for debuggability, applied consistently.

Shared calculations

Three calculations are consumed by more than one feature and exist as pure functions with no repository access, so they can be unit-tested and imported rather than reimplemented:

Calculation | Owner | Consumed by
classifyWorkload(estimatedHours, capacity) | AllocationService | Team dashboard, company overview, overload risk
computeBlockedStates(taskIds) | DependencyService | Task views, priority scoring, blocked-task risk
calculateScore(task, context) | PriorityService | Recommendations, task sorting

Alongside these, two definitions must be written once and reused: overdue (past due date and not DONE) and effort variance (actual against estimated hours).

If any of these gets re-typed inline somewhere, the dashboard and the risk panel will eventually disagree with each other — and a contradiction between two screens is very hard to diagnose from a screenshot.

Derived state is computed, not stored

Goal progress, workload utilisation, blocked state, priority scores and risks are all calculated on read.

The alternative — storing them — means invalidating from every write path that could affect them. Goal progress alone would need updating on task creation, status change and deletion. At this data volume the calculation is cheap. If it ever becomes a bottleneck, cache it; do not denormalise it.

Performance notes

The repository layer exists mainly to keep aggregate queries honest. Two rules:

- Listing N goals must not fire N count queries — use one grouped query keyed by goal
- Team workload must run in constant query count regardless of member count
- Left join from members when building allocation tables, so an employee with zero tasks still appears; an inner join silently drops exactly the row a resource dashboard exists to show

Related pages

- Data Model — entities and relationships
- Architecture Decision Records — what was chosen and why

pages.title: TrackIt — Architecture Decision Records
pages.content:
Each record states the context, the options considered, the decision, and what follows from it. Records are not edited once accepted — if a decision changes, a new record supersedes the old one.

ID | Decision | Status
ADR-001 | Modular monolith instead of microservices | Accepted
ADR-002 | Layered design pattern within each module | Accepted
ADR-003 | TypeORM as the ORM | Accepted
ADR-004 | Derived values computed on read, not stored | Accepted
ADR-005 | Team membership cardinality | Proposed
ADR-006 | Single assignee per task | Proposed
ADR-007 | Manual and derived blocked state coexist | Proposed

ADR-001 — Modular monolith instead of microservices

Status: Accepted

Context. TrackIt has eight functional areas that could plausibly be separate services. The build is short and run by a very small team.

Options. Microservices per domain; a modular monolith; an unstructured monolith.

Decision. A modular monolith with clear internal module boundaries.

Why. Distributed services carry deployment, networking, and observability costs that buy nothing at this size. All eight modules share one database and one transaction boundary anyway — splitting them would mean inventing distributed transactions to solve a problem that does not currently exist.

Consequences. One deployable, one database, straightforward local development. Modules can be extracted later if a real scaling or ownership reason appears. The discipline of the boundaries has to be maintained by convention rather than enforced by the network.

ADR-002 — Layered design pattern within each module

Status: Accepted

Context. A monolith without internal structure becomes a monolith with business logic scattered through route handlers.

Decision. Every module is split into controller, service, repository and entity. Controllers never touch repositories. Business rules live in services. Cross-module reads go through the other module's service.

Why. The layering is what makes shared calculations possible. Three calculations — workload classification, blocked state, priority scoring — are each consumed by two or three features. Putting them in services as pure functions means they are written once, unit-tested, and imported rather than re-typed.

Consequences. More files per feature. In exchange, business logic is testable without HTTP, and the dashboard cannot disagree with the risk panel because both call the same function. Authorisation gets a fixed home: role at the route, scope in the service.

ADR-003 — TypeORM as the ORM

Status: Accepted

Context. The original technology notes said "Prisma or Drizzle" without choosing.

Decision. TypeORM.

Consequences. Entities are decorated classes, and migrations are generated from them. The repository layer wraps TypeORM query builders, so the ORM choice stays contained: if it changes later, repositories are the only layer that has to move.

ADR-004 — Derived values computed on read, not stored

Status: Accepted

Context. Goal progress, employee utilisation, blocked state, priority scores and risks are all functions of other data. Each could be stored as a column and kept up to date.

Options. Store and invalidate on write; compute on every read; compute and cache.

Decision. Compute on read.

Why. Storing means invalidating from every write path that could affect the value. Goal progress alone would need updating on task creation, status change and deletion — three paths, each a chance to drift. Drifted derived data is hard to notice and harder to explain.

Consequences. Reads do more work, which is acceptable at this data volume. Aggregate queries must be written carefully: one grouped query per list, never N+1. If read performance becomes a genuine problem, add caching — do not denormalise.

ADR-005 — Team membership cardinality

Status: Proposed — blocks the first migration

Context. The source requirements contradict themselves. The relationship diagram states User belongs to Team, singular. A team_members join table implies many-to-many.

Options.

One team per user — add a unique constraint on TeamMember.userId. A person's weekly capacity belongs unambiguously to one team, so the allocation dashboard needs no splitting rule.

Many teams per user — no constraint. More realistic, but capacity is then shared across teams and every allocation figure needs a rule for dividing it, which the requirements never specify.

Recommendation. One team per user. The realism gained is not worth the ambiguity introduced into every downstream dashboard.

Consequences if one team. Simpler queries, unambiguous utilisation, and a constraint that would be painful to remove later. Moving to many-to-many afterwards would mean revisiting every allocation query.

Related: TRACKIT-17

ADR-006 — Single assignee per task

Status: Proposed — blocks the first migration

Context. The requirements say to create a TaskAssignment model "if multiple assignees are allowed", leaving the question open.

Recommendation. A single assignee via Task.assigneeId.

Why. The employee-facing feature is "view my assigned tasks", which is unambiguous with one owner. Time logging forbids unassigned tasks — with multiple assignees, "assigned to me" becomes a join rather than a column. Workload divides estimated hours per person, and shared ownership needs a splitting rule the requirements never give.

Consequences. If multiple assignees are wanted later, TaskAssignment must be added before the allocation dashboards are built. Retrofitting it afterwards means rewriting every allocation query.

Related: TRACKIT-21

ADR-007 — Manual and derived blocked state coexist

Status: Proposed

Context. BLOCKED exists as a manually-set task status. Dependencies introduce a second, computed notion of blocked: a task with an unfinished prerequisite. Two sources of truth for one idea.

Options. Derived overrides manual; manual wins; treat them as separate concepts.

Recommendation. Separate concepts. status stays human-controlled; a computed isBlocked sits alongside it. A task is unavailable if either is true.

Why. They are genuinely different. "Waiting on TASK-104" and "blocked because the vendor hasn't replied" are both real states, and collapsing them loses information. It also avoids a background process rewriting statuses that humans set deliberately.

Consequences. The interface must show both clearly, or users will be confused about why a task looks blocked. The −40 penalty in the priority formula must apply to the same definition the interface displays.

Related: TRACKIT-32

Still undecided

Not yet significant enough for their own records, but they need values before the code that uses them is written:

- Maximum daily hours for a timesheet entry — suggested 12
- Duplicate timesheet entries: reject, or add to the existing entry — suggested add
- Goal importance scale — suggested High +20, Medium +10, Low +5
- Effort overrun threshold for raising a risk — suggested 120%
- Deadline-approaching window — suggested 3 days
- "No recent progress" window — suggested 5 days

pages.title: TrackIt — Data Model
pages.content:
Tables

users
teams
team_members
goals
tasks
task_dependencies
timesheet_entries
activity_logs
notifications

Relationships

Team
 ├── has many TeamMembers
 ├── has one TeamLead
 └── has many Goals

Goal
 └── has many Tasks

Task
 ├── belongs to Goal
 ├── assigned to User
 ├── has many TimesheetEntries
 └── depends on other Tasks

User
 ├── belongs to Team
 ├── has assigned Tasks
 └── has TimesheetEntries

Entities

User

id, email (unique), passwordHash, name, role, createdAt, updatedAt

Role: SUPER_ADMIN | TEAM_LEAD | EMPLOYEE

Passwords are stored only as bcrypt hashes. No endpoint returns passwordHash.

Team

id, name (unique), description, teamLeadId (nullable FK → User), weeklyCapacityHours (default 40), createdAt, updatedAt

Capacity sits on the team rather than being a hard-coded constant, which is what makes the workload bands configurable. A team is created with a null lead because the lead must exist as a user first.

TeamMember

id, teamId, userId, joinedAt — unique on (teamId, userId)

Goal

id, teamId (FK), title, description, startDate, deadline, status, importance, createdById, createdAt, updatedAt

Status: PLANNED | ACTIVE | COMPLETED | CANCELLED

importance feeds the priority formula. Status is set manually, not derived — deriving COMPLETED from task counts would conflict with CANCELLED being a deliberate human act.

Task

id, goalId (FK), title, description, status, priority, estimatedHours, dueDate, assigneeId (nullable FK), businessImpact, priorityScore (nullable), createdAt, updatedAt

Status: TODO | IN_PROGRESS | BLOCKED | DONE
Priority: LOW | MEDIUM | HIGH

estimatedHours is the hinge field of the whole application: entered here, compared against recorded time, drives the workload bands, and triggers the overrun risk. It must be positive; zero and negatives are rejected at validation.

businessImpact and priorityScore are added at creation but stay unused until prioritisation is built — placed early to avoid a migration on a table that will already hold data.

TaskDependency

id, taskId, dependsOnTaskId, createdAt — unique on (taskId, dependsOnTaskId)

Direction: a row means taskId is blocked by dependsOnTaskId. This reading is stated once and never restated differently.

Constraints: no self-reference, no duplicate edges, no cycles, and both tasks must belong to the same team. Cycle detection runs before the insert, inside the same transaction — insert-then-check leaves a window where a cycle exists in the database.

TimesheetEntry

id, employeeId (FK), taskId (FK), workDate, hoursSpent, workNote, submissionStatus, createdAt, updatedAt

Indexed on (employeeId, workDate) — every dashboard query filters on that pair.

Rules: the task must be assigned to the employee; hours must be positive and within the daily maximum; the day's total across all tasks stays within that maximum; no future dates. Creation and edit paths share one validator, or an edit can bypass rules that creation enforces.

submissionStatus exists but no approval workflow is in scope.

ActivityLog

id, actorId, entityType, entityId, action, oldValue, newValue, teamId, createdAt

Indexed on (teamId, createdAt) and (entityType, entityId).

Written from services rather than middleware or database triggers, because only the service knows that status: TODO → IN_PROGRESS means "started work" rather than a column update. A logging failure must never fail the operation it describes.

Notification

id, userId, type, message, entityType, entityId, isRead, createdAt

In-app only. Generated synchronously at the triggering event; there is no scheduler, so deadline-approaching notifications fire when something else prompts a check.

Fields that are not columns

These are calculated on read and never stored:

Value | Derived from
Goal progress % | completed tasks / total tasks
Employee utilisation % | estimated hours on active tasks / team capacity
Task blocked state | any prerequisite not DONE
Task priority score | the published scoring formula
Effort variance | recorded hours vs estimatedHours
Risks | the eight risk conditions

Unresolved

Can a user belong to more than one team? The relationship diagram says one; the team_members join table implies many. This must be settled before the first migration — see the Architecture Decision Records page.

pages.title: Introduction
pages.content:
TrackIt is a company-wide task and resource tracking system. Teams have goals, goals break into tasks, tasks are assigned to employees, and employees log time against them. Managers see progress, workload and delivery risk in one place instead of across three spreadsheets.

This space holds the product and engineering documentation. Work is tracked separately in Jira project TRACKIT, as six epics and 27 stories.

The problem

Software companies track tasks, time, goals and team allocation in separate tools. Because the data is split, managers cannot answer basic questions: what is each team working on, is a project on schedule, who is overloaded, which work is at risk. Employees have the mirror problem — work arrives through chat and meetings, with no single place to see assignments or record effort.

The model

Everything hangs off one chain:

Company → Teams → Goals → Tasks → Assignees → Timesheets → Dashboards

A goal is a body of work with a deadline, owned by one team. Tasks are the assignable units beneath it. Time is recorded against tasks. Everything a dashboard shows is derived from that chain rather than stored.

Three roles: Super Admin builds the company structure and sees everything; Team Lead owns their team's goals, tasks and assignments; Employee sees only their own work and logs their own time.

How it is built

A modular monolith — Node, Express and TypeScript on PostgreSQL with TypeORM, React on the front, JWT for authentication. Every module follows the same four layers: controller, service, repository, entity.

Delivery runs across six sprints, one epic each, sequenced by data dependency rather than preference. You cannot log time against a task that does not exist, and you cannot calculate workload without estimates and recorded hours.

Documentation

Product and planning

Product Overview — what TrackIt is, the problem it solves, the domain chain, the three roles, and what success looks like. Start here.

Product Requirements — the scoped feature set, epic by epic, with the permissions matrix and an explicit out-of-scope list. The reference for scope questions during the build.

Roadmap — six sprints with goals and dates, story distribution, sequencing constraints, and the order to cut things in if time runs short.

Engineering and architecture

System Architecture — stack, the modular monolith, the layered pattern and its rules, the authorisation model, and the shared calculations that must never be duplicated.

Data Model — tables, entities and their fields, relationships, and which values are computed on read rather than stored.

Architecture Decision Records — seven records covering what was chosen and why. Four accepted, three still proposed.

Open decisions

Two questions remain unanswered and block the first entity migration:

1. Can an employee belong to more than one team? The relationship model says one; the join table implies many. Affects every allocation calculation.
2. Can a task have more than one assignee? Currently modelled as a single assignee. Changing it later means rewriting every allocation query.

Both are recorded as ADR-005 and ADR-006, marked Proposed. Three smaller decisions — the duplicate-timesheet rule, manual versus derived blocked state, and confirmation of the configured thresholds — can wait until the story that needs them.

Note on this project

TrackIt is a demonstration application. It is built to exercise a realistic set of engineering problems — role-based access, effort tracking, dependency graphs, derived metrics — and to produce a body of interlinked project data across code, tickets and documentation.

pages.title: TrackIt — Phases
pages.content:
Delivery runs in three phases across six sprints, one epic per sprint. The sequence is dictated by data dependencies rather than preference — each phase's output is the next phase's input.

Phase 1 — Core task management

Sprints 1–2 · Epics 1–2 · TRACKIT-12 → 23

Establishes the company structure and the core domain. A Super Admin creates teams, users and leads; a Team Lead creates goals, breaks them into tasks and assigns them; an Employee sees their own work and moves it through statuses.

This phase also sets the patterns everything else copies: the four-layer module shape, the authorisation model, and the error contract.

Deliverable. A working role-based task management application. Structure, goals, tasks, assignments, deadlines and progress can all be managed.

Phase 2 — Timesheets and resource management

Sprints 3–4 · Epics 3–4 · TRACKIT-24 → 30

Turns the system from a task list into an effort-tracking tool. Employees record daily hours against assigned tasks; every task shows actual effort against its estimate; managers see who is overloaded and who is free.

The workload calculation introduced here is used by three later features, so it is built once as a pure function rather than inline in a dashboard.

Deliverable. Employees record daily work; leads and admins can inspect timesheets, task effort, team workload and resource allocation.

Phase 3 — Prioritisation, risk and advanced features

Sprints 5–6 · Epics 5–6 · TRACKIT-31 → 38

Makes the application advisory rather than merely descriptive. Tasks declare dependencies, cycles are rejected, blocked work is identified, and available work is ranked with explanations. Eight risk conditions surface delivery problems before deadlines are missed.

Risk detection consumes all four preceding epics, which is why it is last.

Deliverable. The application ranks tasks, detects blockers, highlights resource and deadline risks, records important changes, and provides management dashboards.

Phase summary

Phase | Sprints | Epics | Stories | Focus
1 | 1–2 | 1–2 | 12 | Structure, goals, tasks, assignment
2 | 3–4 | 3–4 | 7 | Time recording, workload, dashboards
3 | 5–6 | 5–6 | 8 | Dependencies, ranking, risk, audit

Sequencing constraints

These are hard, not preferences:

- Nothing can be authorised until identity exists — Phase 1 blocks everything
- Time attaches to tasks, so tasks precede timesheets
- Workload needs both estimates and recorded hours, so allocation follows time recording
- Priority scoring needs blocked state, which needs dependencies
- Risk detection consumes all four preceding epics and must be last

Everything in Phases 1 and 2 is load-bearing. If time runs short, cut from Phase 3 — optional polish first, then search, then notifications, then activity logging. Risk detection is what makes Phase 3 meaningful and is the last thing to go.

Detail

See the Roadmap below for sprint dates, goals, story distribution and the full cut order.

Purpose. This page explains what TrackIt Phase 2 delivered and how it works end to end — from role-specific React screens, through the REST API and service layer, down to the PostgreSQL queries and schema. It is written for technical stakeholders: engineering, architecture, QA, and technically minded product owners who need to understand the delivered system without reading every source file. Scope of Phase 2: Timesheets and resource management across the Effort and Insight contexts — employee time recording, correction and history, task effort variance, Team Lead timesheet visibility, workload classification, team dashboards, and the Super Admin company overview. It covers Sprints 3–4, Epics 3–4, and TRACKIT-24 through TRACKIT-30. This document describes the system as built, not the original ticket aspirations or the full product vision. - Phase 1 — Core Task Management: End-to-End Technical Overview - TrackIt — Phases - Domain source of truth: docs/DOMAIN.md - Engineering rules: AGENTS.md - Module contracts: backend/src/modules/timesheets/README.md and backend/src/modules/dashboards/README.md 1. Where Phase 2 sits TrackIt is delivered in three phases. Phase 1 established who exists, how people are grouped, what work exists, and who owns it. Phase 2 adds actual effort and turns those operational records into workload insight. Shared calculations and invariants 6.1 Daily time validation For a new entry: new daily total = existing hours across all tasks for the date + submitted hours For an edit: adjusted daily total = current daily total - old entry hours + replacement hours The submitted or replacement value must be finite, greater than zero, and no more than 12 hours. The resulting daily total must also be no more than 12 hours. 6.2 Duplicate time logging The resolved duplicate rule is upsert by addition. If the same employee logs time again for the same task and work date: - no second row is created; - the new hours are added to the existing row; - a non-empty work note is appended on a new line; - an empty new note preserves the existing note; - the API returns 200 instead of 201. The database unique constraint protects the same invariant at the storage level. 6.3 History ranges Personal and team timesheet history use inclusive YYYY-MM-DD ranges. - Both from and to must be supplied together. - From must be on or before to. - The inclusive range cannot exceed 90 days. - Omitting the range uses the current UTC Monday-to-Sunday week. 6.4 Effort variance variance hours = actual recorded hours - estimated hours variance percent = variance hours / estimated hours × 100 Status | Rule UNDER_ESTIMATE | actual < estimate ON_ESTIMATE | actual = estimate OVER_ESTIMATE | estimate < actual ≤ 120% of estimate OVERRUN | actual > 120% of estimate Exactly 120% is OVER_ESTIMATE; OVERRUN begins above the configured threshold. Division is guarded when an estimate is zero even though normal task creation rejects non-positive estimates. 6.5 Utilisation and workload utilisation = estimated hours on active tasks / weekly capacity hours × 100 Active means task status is anything other than DONE. A task manually marked BLOCKED still occupies capacity. Active-task estimates always compare against one weekly capacity baseline, even if the selected recorded-hours range covers several weeks. This is deliberate: recorded hours are historical activity; estimates are the current assignment. 6.7 Dashboard task definitions - Completed: status is DONE. - Blocked: persisted task status is BLOCKED. - Overdue: due date is before today and status is not DONE. - Goal progress: completed task count divided by total task count, inherited from Phase 1. Super Admin - / — automatically renders the Company Dashboard. - Company KPI cards, team comparison, and company employee allocation. - Team and date filters are server-side. - Employee selection filters the returned employee table client-side. - Team rows link to /teams/:id/dashboard. - Task Details includes effort visibility. - Super Admin cannot use the Team-Lead-only team-timesheet route. All screens use the shared API client and Phase 1 authentication context. Loading, empty, and error states are presented in the screen that owns the request. 10. Query and performance design Phase 2 is the first aggregation-heavy part of TrackIt. The implementation follows the repository’s query rules deliberately. Timesheet queries - Ownership-sensitive lists filter employee ID in SQL. - Team history filters through task → goal → team in SQL. - Daily and per-task history totals use GROUP BY, not JavaScript accumulation. - Task effort totals can accept task ID batches and return a keyed map. - Empty task sets skip the aggregate query. Allocation queries - The query starts from teams and team_members. - Tasks and timesheets are left joined, preserving members with zero work. - Active estimates and recorded hours are aggregated separately so a task/entry join cannot multiply totals. - Date filters appear only in the timesheet metrics. - Team, goal, and date filters compose with AND. - The company read model uses one SQL query regardless of team or member count. - Team summaries use a constant number of aggregate reads regardless of member count. - Goal progress continues to use grouped Phase 1 task counts rather than one count query per goal. Why calculations remain in services Repositories return facts: estimates, counts, recorded hours, capacity, statuses, and dates. Services apply domain meaning: utilisation, workload classification, overdue state, effort variance, and response projections. This keeps SQL focused on set operations while preserving one reusable definition of each business rule. 11. Running and verification Local verification commands cd backend npm test npm run build cd ../frontend npm test npm run build Verification at publication Check | Result Backend tests | 262 passed, 0 failed Frontend tests | 8 passed, 0 failed Backend TypeScript build | Passed Frontend TypeScript + Vite production build | Passed The backend suite covers route roles, scope rejection, time ownership, duplicate upsert, future dates, hour validation, daily limits, history ranges, task effort, workload thresholds, zero-task employees, composed filters, constant-query repository shapes, KPIs, and default-week behavior. The frontend suite currently covers shared display, sorting, and navigation helpers. The production build verifies the complete Phase 2 React route/component graph type-checks and bundles successfully. High-value acceptance checks 1. Employee logs twice against the same task/date: one row remains, hours add, notes append. 2. Employee tries to log another employee’s task: 403 and no write. 3. Edit would push the day above 12 hours: 400 and original entry remains. 4. Team Lead requests another team’s timesheets or dashboard: 403. 5. Employee with no tasks appears in allocation as AVAILABLE with zero values. 6. Changing the dashboard date range changes recorded hours only. 7. Company totals equal sums of the returned per-team figures. 8. Team and goal backend filters compose rather than replace each other. 9. DONE tasks leave active estimates and are never overdue. 10. Task effort above 120% receives OVERRUN; exactly 120% remains OVER_ESTIMATE. 12. Known limitations and Phase 3 handoff Deliberate Phase 2 limits - No timesheet approval workflow. submissionStatus is always SUBMITTED. - No standalone personal history UI. The personal history, edit and delete APIs exist, but the React application does not yet expose a My Timesheet page. - No derived-value storage. Workload, utilisation, variance, progress, and dashboard totals are calculated on read. - No future capacity planning. Allocation represents current active-task commitments against one weekly capacity. - No scaling by date-range length. Longer ranges widen recorded-hour history only. - No cost, billing, payroll, invoicing, timers, or automatic tracking. - No CSV export. - No automatic assignment or scheduling. - No dependency-derived blocking. The blocked KPI uses the task’s persisted BLOCKED status. - No risk notifications. Phase 2 displays overdue and overloaded conditions but does not turn them into risk records or alerts. Small interface gaps to be aware of - The company backend accepts a goalId filter; the current UI does not expose it. - The company employee selector is a client-side table filter rather than an API filter. - Super Admin can inspect task effort and dashboards but cannot open the Team-Lead-only team-timesheet route. - Jira parent Epics 3 and 4 remain To Do even though all seven Phase 2 stories are Done. Phase 3 reuses these foundations Phase 3 should import rather than retype: - classifyWorkload for overloaded-employee risk; - isTaskOverdue for overdue-task risk; - effort totals and the configured 120% threshold for estimate-overrun risk; - Phase 1 goal progress for deadline/progress risk; - the same query-level team/company scope patterns for risk dashboards. Phase 2 therefore changes TrackIt from a record of assigned work into an operational management tool: employees record actual effort, Team Leads see delivery and workload for their team, and Super Admins see the same consistent calculations across the company.

sample_chunks.title: TrackIt — Product Overview
sample_chunks.content:
Space: TrackIt (TR)
Page: TrackIt — Product Overview

Content:
What TrackIt is

TrackIt is a company-wide work tracking system. It connects the organisation's structure to the work being done and the time being spent, so that managers can answer questions about progress and capacity from one place instead of three spreadsheets.

The first version is a task and resource tracking application. It can later expand into a full company project-tracking platform.

The problem

Software companies commonly track tasks, employee time, project goals and team allocation in separate tools. Because the data is split, managers struggle to answer basic questions:

- What is each team currently working on?
- Is a project on schedule?
- Which employees are overloaded, and which are underutilised?
- How much time has been spent on each task?
- Which tasks are delayed or high risk?
- Are team goals progressing toward their deadlines?

Employees have a parallel problem: work arrives through chat messages and meetings, with no single place to see what is assigned to them or record what they did.

The model

Everything in TrackIt hangs off one chain:

Company
  └── Teams
       └── Team Goals
            └── Tasks
                 └── Assigned Employees
                      └── Daily Timesheets
                           └── Progress and Resource Dashboards

A goal is a body of work with a deadline, owned by one team. Tasks are the assignable units under a goal. Time is recorded against tasks. Everything a dashboard shows is derived from that chain.

Roles

Role | What they do
Super Admin | Creates teams, users and team leads. Sees every team, goal, task and timesheet, plus company-wide resource allocation.
Team Lead | Creates goals for their team, breaks them into tasks, assigns members, sets priorities, and monitors their team's progress, timesheets and workload.
Employee | Sees only their assigned tasks. Updates task status, records daily time with a short work note, and views their own timesheet history.

A Manager, in the language of the original requirements, is served by the Team Lead and Super Admin views rather than being a separate role.

What success looks like

TrackIt is working when:

- A Super Admin can build the company structure and see allocation across every team
- A Team Lead can create a goal with a deadline, assign the work, and see who is overloaded
- An Employee has one screen showing what is assigned to them and one place to log time
- Overdue, blocked and high-risk work is visible without anyone having to go looking for it

Related pages

- Product Requirements — the scoped feature set
- Roadmap — phasing and sequence
- System Architecture — how it is built

Note on this project

TrackIt is a demonstration application. It is built to exercise a realistic set of engineering problems — role-based access, effort tracking, dependency graphs, derived metrics — and to produce a body of interlinked project data.

sample_chunks.content:
Space: TrackIt (TR)
Page: TrackIt — Product Requirements

Content:
Purpose

This page defines what TrackIt does, feature by feature, and what it deliberately does not do. It is the reference for scope questions during the build.

Delivery is organised into six epics, tracked in Jira project TRACKIT.

Permissions summary

Capability | Super Admin | Team Lead | Employee
Create teams and users | Yes | No | No
Assign team leads | Yes | No | No
Create goals and tasks | Yes | Own team | No
Assign tasks | Yes | Own team | No
Update task status | Yes | Own team | Own tasks
Log time | — | — | Own tasks
View timesheets | All | Own team | Own only
View allocation dashboards | Company-wide | Own team | No

The rule that governs every row: scope is enforced server-side, in the query. Hiding a control in the interface is not access control.

Epic 1 — Team and user administration

A Super Admin creates users with a name, email, password and role, creates teams, adds employees to teams, and designates exactly one team lead per team. Login uses JWT; role-based middleware guards every protected route.

Accepted when: the Super Admin can build the full structure; exactly one lead exists per team; an employee calling an admin endpoint receives 403.

Epic 2 — Goals, tasks and assignment

A Team Lead creates a goal for their team with a start date, deadline and importance, then breaks it into tasks carrying a priority, an estimated effort and a due date. Tasks are assigned to members of that same team. Employees see their assigned tasks on one screen and move them between statuses. Each goal shows a progress percentage derived from its completed tasks.

Statuses — Goal: PLANNED, ACTIVE, COMPLETED, CANCELLED. Task: TODO, IN_PROGRESS, BLOCKED, DONE. Priority: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH.

Accepted when: a lead can create a goal and tasks and assign them; an employee sees only their own tasks and can change their status; goal progress reflects completed tasks.

Epic 3 — Employee timesheets

An employee records hours against an assigned task for a given date, with a short work note. Time cannot be logged against a task that is not assigned to them. Hours are validated against a configured daily maximum and cannot be zero, negative or future-dated. Employees can correct or delete their own entries and review their history over a date range. Each task shows total recorded time against its estimate.

Accepted when: time can be logged only against assigned tasks; invalid hours are rejected; task detail shows actual against estimated effort; no employee can see another's entries.

Epic 4 — Resource allocation and dashboards

One calculation determines each employee's utilisation:

utilisation = estimated hours on active tasks / weekly capacity

  0–60%  Available
 61–90%  Balanced
   >90%  Overloaded

Weekly capacity is configurable per team, defaulting to 40 hours. An active task is one that is not DONE; blocked tasks still count, because blocked work still occupies a person.

The Team Dashboard shows goal and task KPIs plus a per-employee workload table. The Super Admin sees the same shape company-wide, with filters for team, employee and date range.

Accepted when: a lead sees allocation for their own team only; the Super Admin sees all teams; overloaded and available employees are visible; an employee with no tasks still appears in the table.

Epic 5 — Prioritisation and dependencies

Tasks can declare that they depend on other tasks. Self-dependencies and circular dependencies are rejected. A task is blocked when a prerequisite is not yet DONE.

Ranking uses a fixed, published formula:

Priority score =
  Business priority + Deadline urgency
+ Dependency impact + Goal importance
- Blocked penalty

High priority:       +30      Due within 2 days:   +30
Medium priority:     +20      Due within 7 days:   +20
Low priority:        +10      Due later:            +5

Blocks another task: +10 each
Currently blocked:   -40

Every recommendation carries the reasons behind its score. An unexplained ranking is one nobody trusts, so the explanation is part of the feature rather than decoration on it.

Accepted when: cycles are rejected; blocked tasks are identified; available tasks are ranked; a lead can see why a task scored as it did.

Epic 6 — Risk, audit and search

Eight conditions raise a risk: task overdue, high-priority task blocked, goal deadline approaching, goal progress below expectation, unassigned task, employee overloaded, actual hours exceeding estimate, and no recent progress. Risks are grouped by severity and link through to the underlying record.

Significant changes — status, assignment, priority, timesheets, goals, dependencies — are written to an activity log. Tasks are searchable and filterable, and users are notified in-app when work is assigned to them.

Accepted when: risks appear in one place with severity; important actions appear in history; tasks can be searched within the caller's scope.

Out of scope

- Email, Slack or push notifications — in-app only
- Approval workflows for timesheets
- Billing, invoicing, payroll or cost rates
- Predictive or machine-learning risk scoring; all rules are deterministic
- Automatic assignment or scheduling — the system recommends, a human decides
- Password reset, email verification, SSO, multi-tenancy
- Critical-path analysis and Gantt scheduling

Open decisions

Five choices remain open and are recorded on the Architecture Decision Records page. Two of them block the first migration: whether a user can belong to more than one team, and whether a task can have more than one assignee.

sample_chunks.content:
Space: TrackIt (TR)
Page: TrackIt — Roadmap

Content:
Shape of the plan

Six sprints, one epic each. Each sprint is scheduled as one week, though the intent is to complete most in two to three days.

The sequence is dictated by data dependencies rather than preference: you cannot log time against a task that does not exist, and you cannot calculate workload without estimates and recorded hours. Each sprint's output is the next sprint's input.

Sprints

# | Dates | Sprint | Goal
1 | Aug 10–14 | Foundation & Org Structure | A Super Admin can log in, build the company structure, and every role boundary is enforced server-side. The layered pattern is established and copyable.
2 | Aug 17–21 | Goals, Tasks & Assignment | A Team Lead can create a goal, break it into tasks and assign them; an Employee sees only their own work. Goal progress reflects reality.
3 | Aug 24–28 | Time Recording | Employees record daily hours against assigned tasks, and every task shows actual effort against its estimate.
4 | Aug 31–Sep 4 | Resource Visibility | A Team Lead can see who is overloaded and who is free; a Super Admin can compare teams. One workload calculation, used everywhere.
5 | Sep 7–11 | Prioritisation & Dependencies | Tasks can depend on each other without cycles, and the system recommends what to do next with reasons a human can check.
6 | Sep 14–18 | Risk, Audit & Polish | Delivery risks surface in one place before deadlines are missed, significant changes are recorded, and the app is demo-ready.

Deliverable at each phase

Phase 1 (Sprints 1–2) — a working role-based task management application. Structure, goals, tasks, assignments, deadlines and progress can all be managed.

Phase 2 (Sprints 3–4) — employees record daily work; leads and admins can inspect timesheets, task effort, team workload and resource allocation.

Phase 3 (Sprints 5–6) — the application ranks tasks, detects blockers, highlights resource and deadline risks, records important changes, and provides management dashboards.

Story distribution

Sprint | Stories | Jira
1 | 7 | TRACKIT-12 → 18
2 | 5 | TRACKIT-19 → 23
3 | 4 | TRACKIT-24 → 27
4 | 3 | TRACKIT-28 → 30
5 | 4 | TRACKIT-31 → 34
6 | 4 | TRACKIT-35 → 38

Sprint 1 is the heaviest: it carries the whole project bootstrap alongside authentication and team administration. It is the sprint most likely to overrun, and the scaffold work is the part to timebox hardest.

Sprint 4 is the lightest at three stories, but two of them are dashboards, and dashboard work tends to expand to fill the time available.

Sequencing constraints

These are hard, not preferences:

- Nothing can be authorised until identity exists (Sprint 1 blocks everything)
- Time attaches to tasks, so tasks precede timesheets
- Workload needs both estimates and recorded hours, so allocation follows time recording
- Priority scoring needs blocked state, which needs dependencies
- Risk detection consumes all four preceding epics and must be last

If time runs short

Cut in this order, from the least costly:

1. Optional polish — dark mode, drag-and-drop, CSV export, charts
2. Search and filtering
3. Notifications
4. Activity logging

Risk detection is what makes Phase 3 meaningful and is the last thing to go. Everything in Phases 1 and 2 is load-bearing.
